think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 17-year-old girl presents with acute hypoxic respiratory failure (SpO2 74%), tachycardia (167 bpm), tachypnea (59 breaths/min), and fever immediately following incision and drainage of a perianal abscess. Physical examination reveals a confluence of pulmonary rales, meningismus (neck stiffness, positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs), and a fluctuating subcutaneous back mass. Despite being maintained on a prolonged multi-drug antimicrobial regimen for chronic pleurisy and having recently recovered from viral pneumonitis (COVID-19), her fulminant multi-system presentation creates diagnostic tension between post-surgical pyogenic bacterial sepsis with septic emboli, inflammatory bowel disease with extraintestinal manifestations, and breakthrough disseminated mycobacterial infection facilitated by immune exhaustion (CD4 count 234/µL).

2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission clinical evaluation concludes after physical examination, triage vital signs, baseline blood tests (neutrophilic leukocytosis, normocytic anemia, elevated CRP, elevated serum adenosine deaminase, low CD4 count, negative HIV/viral hepatitis), routine microbiological sputum and blood cultures, and bedside chest radiography showing diffuse bilateral pulmonary foci and small pleural effusions, strictly prior to post-seizure lumbar puncture, cerebrospinal fluid next-generation sequencing, endoscopic evaluation, and percutaneous aspiration of the cold abscess.

3. Differential Distinctions: Acute pyogenic bacteremia with metastatic abscesses is ruled out by sterile blood, sputum, and cerebrospinal fluid bacterial cultures. Crohn's disease with perianal fistulizing disease and systemic inflammation is ruled out by subsequent identification of acid-fast bacilli in the back abscess aspirate and response to adjusted anti-mycobacterial therapy. Aseptic meningitis is excluded by metagenomic next-generation sequencing establishing central nervous system involvement.
case_prompt:
A 17-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with 2 days of intermittent fevers (peak temperature 38.5°C), progressive respiratory distress, and dyspnea developing shortly after undergoing surgical incision and drainage of a perianal abscess at an outside hospital. Past medical history was notable for chronic exudative pleurisy diagnosed the preceding year, for which she had been maintained on a prolonged, multi-agent antimicrobial regimen. In addition, she had documented SARS-CoV-2 infection diagnosed via real-time molecular assay one month prior to presentation. She had no history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or hepatitis B or C infection.

On physical examination, the patient was in severe respiratory distress and critically hypoxic. Vital signs revealed a body temperature of 37.8°C, heart rate of 167 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 59 breaths per minute, blood pressure of 132/92 mmHg, and an ambient room air oxygen saturation of 74%. Chest auscultation demonstrated bilateral diffuse moist rales. Neurological examination showed meningeal irritation signs, including mild neck stiffness, a positive Kernig's sign, and a positive Brudzinski's sign. Examination of the back revealed a fluctuant, non-tender subcutaneous mass in the left lower back region, and the perianal area showed a healing surgical wound from the recent drainage procedure. Other organ systems were normal.

Emergency laboratory testing revealed leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 15.91 × 10⁹/L (reference 4.1–11.0 × 10⁹/L) and a neutrophil predominance of 14.34 × 10⁹/L (reference 1.8–8.3 × 10⁹/L), normocytic anemia with a hemoglobin of 86 g/L (reference 114–145 g/L), and an elevated C-reactive protein of 89.98 mg/L (reference < 5.0 mg/L). Serum adenosine deaminase was elevated at 24.1 U/L (reference < 20 U/L). Immunological flow cytometry showed severe CD4+ T-cell lymphopenia with an absolute CD4 count of 234/µL (reference 554–1109/µL). Serological tests for HIV and hepatitis B and C were negative. Multiple sets of blood and sputum cultures, as well as initial sputum smears for bacteria and fungi, were negative. Bedside chest radiography demonstrated diffuse bilateral infectious pulmonary infiltrates accompanied by mild bilateral pleural effusions.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Acute Pyogenic Sepsis and Bacterial Pneumonia with Septic Emboli
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The sudden acute presentation following perianal abscess surgery with marked neutrophilic leukocytosis and critical hypoxia suggested severe bacterial sepsis; however, standard sputum smears and bacterial/fungal cultures of both sputum and blood were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Considering intermittent fever, sputum smears and sputum and blood cultures of bacteria and fungus were also negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The development of a perianal abscess and fistula, subsequently accompanied by ileal and rectal ulcerations, raised strong suspicion for Crohn's disease, but histopathologic confirmation was precluded by active bleeding and the lesions resolved under modified anti-mycobacterial therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Since there was active bleeding in the terminal ileum, we did not get a biopsy of the lesions, which made it difficult to make a differential diagnosis between intestinal tuberculosis and Crohn's disease.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The definitive turning point occurred when cerebrospinal fluid next-generation sequencing detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis following a generalized seizure, and subsequent percutaneous needle aspiration of the fluctuant subcutaneous lumbar mass yielded purulent fluid that was positive on acid-fast bacilli smear, confirming disseminated tuberculosis involving the meninges, lungs, pleura, intestine, and soft tissues.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Remarkably, Mycobacterium tuberculosis was detected according to the results of NGS, with evidence of high sensitivity and specificity in the diagnosis of tuberculous meningitis.

editor_comments: Distilled in strict compliance with Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Admission prompt removes all explicit references to tuberculosis, anti-TB medications, lumbar puncture findings, NGS, endoscopy, and cold abscess AFB smears while preserving complete admission clinical state and triage data.
